content: Taxus is a genus of yew trees, which are small coniferous trees or shrubs belonging to the family Taxaceae. These trees grow relatively slowly and can live for an exceptionally long time, reaching heights of 1 to 40 meters and trunk diameters of up to 4 meters. The bark of yew trees is reddish, and their leaves are lanceolate, flat, and dark green, measuring 1 to 4 cm in length and 2 to 3 mm in width. The leaves are arranged spirally on the stem, but their bases twist to align the leaves in two flat rows on either side of the stem. The seed cones of yew trees are highly modified structures. Each cone contains a single seed, measuring 4 to 7 mm in length, which is partially surrounded by a modified scale. This scale develops into a soft, bright red, berry-like structure called an aril, which is 8 to 15 mm long and wide and open at one end. The arils mature 6 to 9 months after pollination and are consumed by birds such as thrushes and waxwings. These birds disperse the hard seeds undamaged in their droppings. The maturation of the arils occurs over a period of 2 to 3 months, increasing the likelihood of successful seed dispersal. Male cones of yew trees are globose, measuring 3 to 6 mm in diameter, and release their pollen in early spring. Yew trees are predominantly dioecious, meaning male and female reproductive structures are found on separate trees. However, some individuals may exhibit monoecious characteristics or even change sex over time. All yew species are closely related, and some botanists classify them as subspecies or varieties of a single widespread species, Taxus baccata, which was the first yew described scientifically. Among the most distinct species is the Sumatran Yew (Taxus sumatrana), native to regions from Sumatra and Celebes to southernmost China, characterized by sparse, sickle-shaped yellow-green leaves. The Mexican Yew (Taxus globosa), found in eastern Mexico and extending south to Honduras, has foliage that is intermediate between the Sumatran Yew and other species. Rare species such as the Florida Yew, Mexican Yew, and Pacific Yew are listed as threatened or endangered. All yew species contain highly toxic alkaloids known as taxanes, with slight variations in their chemical structure among species. These alkaloids are present in all parts of the tree except the arils. While the arils are sweet and edible, the seeds they contain are dangerously poisonous. Unlike birds, the human digestive system can break down the seed coat, releasing the toxic taxanes into the body, which can result in fatal outcomes if yew berries are consumed without removing the seeds. Grazing animals, particularly cattle and horses, are also at risk of poisoning after consuming yew leaves, often found dead near yew trees. However, deer are capable of metabolizing the toxins and will freely consume yew foliage. In the wild, extensive browsing by deer often restricts wild yew trees to cliffs and steep slopes that are inaccessible to them. Additionally, the foliage of yew trees serves as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidopteran insects, such as the Willow Beauty moth. Yew wood is reddish-brown with lighter sapwood and is highly elastic. Historically, it was used to craft bows, particularly longbows. Ötzi, the Chalcolithic mummy discovered in the Austrian Alps in 1991, carried an unfinished longbow made of yew wood. In Norse mythology, the god of the bow, Ullr, resided in a place called Ydalir, meaning Yew Dales. Most longbow wood used in northern Europe was imported from Iberia, where climatic conditions favored the growth of knot-free yew wood. The Eihwaz rune (ᛇ) is named after the yew tree and is sometimes associated with the evergreen World Tree, Yggdrasil. Yews are widely used in landscaping and ornamental horticulture. Over 400 cultivars of yew trees have been named, most of which are derived from the European Yew, Japanese Yew, and their hybrid (Taxus × media). Popular cultivars include the Irish Yew (Taxus baccata 'Fastigiata'), a fastigiate form of the European Yew, and various golden-leaved variants collectively known as golden yew. The Pacific Yew (Taxus brevifolia), native to the Pacific Northwest of North America, and the Canada Yew (Taxus canadensis) are sources of paclitaxel, a chemotherapeutic drug used in the treatment of breast and lung cancers. Paclitaxel is also utilized in the production of the Taxus drug-eluting stent by Boston Scientific. Over-harvesting of the Pacific Yew for this drug has led to its classification as an endangered species. However, paclitaxel is now produced semi-synthetically from cultivated yews, reducing the need to harvest wild populations. The more common Canada Yew is also being successfully harvested in northern Ontario, Québec, and New Brunswick, becoming another major source of paclitaxel. Other yew species contain similar compounds with comparable biochemical activity. Docetaxel, an analogue of paclitaxel, is derived from Taxus baccata. Yew trees are often found in church graveyards and are symbolic of sadness. They frequently appear as symbols in the Christian poetry of T.S. Eliot, particularly in his Four Quartets. On January 18, 2008, Botanic Gardens Conservation International, representing botanical gardens in 120 countries, reported that 400 medicinal plants, including yew trees, are at risk of extinction due to over-collection and deforestation. This threatens the discovery of future cures for diseases. Yew trees, specifically their bark, are used to produce cancer drugs like paclitaxel. Other endangered medicinal plants include Hoodia (used for weight loss), half of all Magnolia species (used in Chinese medicine for cancer, dementia, and heart disease), and Autumn Crocus (used for gout).
